## 2. Tool-by-Tool Assessment

### 2.1 eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python)

**Best use case:** Per-pixel processing and analysis of spectrum-image (SI) datacubes, particularly for (S)TEM-EDS. HyperSpy was originally a monolithic Python library for multi-dimensional data analysis in electron microscopy; the EDS/EELS quantification functionality has been refactored into a dedicated extension package called eXSpy (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10).

**Strengths:** HyperSpy/eXSpy operates natively on numpy arrays and integrates directly with the broader Python scientific ecosystem (scipy, scikit-learn, scikit-image, matplotlib). It provides built-in principal component analysis (PCA) and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) for denoising and blind source separation of spectrum images (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). For TEM-EDS, it implements the Cliff–Lorimer k-factor method, which has been used in published quantitative studies of bimetallic nanoparticles (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). It is the strongest of the three tools for automated, large-scale per-pixel spectral processing and is widely used for STEM-EDS quantitative mapping (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7).

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** HyperSpy/eXSpy does not include a validated, built-in ZAF or φ(ρz) matrix correction engine for bulk SEM-EDS quantification, which limits its applicability for the standards-based k-ratio protocol central to rigorous SEM microanalysis (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Published accuracy benchmarks comparable to Newbury & Ritchie's RDEV studies for DTSA-II do not appear to exist for HyperSpy's EDS quantification. Its Cliff–Lorimer approach is appropriate for thin specimens (TEM) but does not account for the absorption and fluorescence corrections required for bulk samples.

**Costs:** Free and open source (Apache/BSD-style license). Computationally efficient for vectorized datacube operations but can demand substantial RAM for very large SI datasets. Requires familiarity with Python and package management (conda/pip), which presents a learning curve for users accustomed to GUI-based microanalysis software. Cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux).

### 2.2 NIST DTSA-II (Java)

**Best use case:** Rigorous, standards-based bulk-specimen SEM-EDS quantitative analysis following the k-ratio/matrix correction protocol, including quantitative compositional mapping of spectrum images (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

**Strengths:** DTSA-II implements multiple linear least squares (MLLS) peak fitting using experimentally measured peak references, enabling robust deconvolution of overlapping peaks and inspection of peak-fitting residual spectra to detect hidden constituents (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22). It employs the XPP φ(ρz) matrix correction algorithm (Pouchou & Pichoir, 1991) as its default, using the Chantler FFAST mass absorption coefficient (MAC) database (Z ≤ 92) supplemented by Sabbatucci coefficients (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). DTSA-II has the most extensive published accuracy validation of the three tools: Newbury & Ritchie (2024) tested 263 concentration measurements for 39 elements in 113 materials at 5 keV and found >98% within ±5% RDEV and 82% within ±2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). At conventional beam energies (E₀ = 20 keV), a database of 122 analyses showed 100% within ±5% RDEV and 89% within ±2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). The raw analytical total (sum of all constituents) typically falls within 0.98–1.02, serving as an independent quality check (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4). For quantitative compositional mapping, DTSA-II applies the full standards-based quantitative analysis procedure at every pixel of a spectrum image, converting raw intensity maps to true concentration maps that remove artifacts such as the Z-dependent continuum background (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26, goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 13-17). Newbury & Ritchie demonstrated this with a Raney nickel alloy example where false Fe contrast in raw intensity maps was eliminated by quantitative processing (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26).

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** Per-pixel quantitative compositional mapping is computationally intensive and requires high count statistics (~1000+ counts per pixel spectrum) for low-variance wt% maps, which can demand long acquisition times (100–10,000 s depending on pixel density) (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26). Scripting is via Jython (Python on Java), which is functional but less ergonomic than native Python for modern data science workflows. The Java desktop application has a moderate learning curve, particularly for managing the standards archive and understanding the analytical workflow conventions (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). DTSA-II uses a single default matrix correction model (XPP), without the multi-model comparison capability of CalcZAF.

**Costs:** Free, open source/open access from NIST. Cross-platform (Java). Moderate computational cost for point analyses; higher for per-pixel mapping of large SI datacubes. The learning curve is moderate-to-steep, as the user must understand both the k-ratio protocol concepts and the DTSA-II software interface.

### 2.3 CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software)

**Best use case:** Standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction with the ability to select from and compare multiple φ(ρz)/ZAF correction models on the same data, particularly useful for batch processing of externally measured k-ratios or assessing model-dependent uncertainties (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23).

**Strengths:** CalcZAF's distinguishing feature is its implementation of multiple matrix correction algorithms — including PAP, XPP, PRZ (PROZA), Armstrong/CITZAF, and others — along with multiple MAC databases (Heinrich, Henke, Chantler) (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). This multi-model capability allows analysts to evaluate the sensitivity of results to the choice of correction algorithm, which is particularly important in challenging analytical situations where the absorption correction is large (e.g., light elements, L-lines, low overvoltage) (rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). Armstrong, Donovan, and Carpenter (2013) specifically documented the use of CalcZAF/TryZAF/CITZAF multi-correction-algorithm programs for estimating uncertainties and improving quantitative analysis of difficult specimens. The Donovan group has also contributed advances in dead-time calibration and k-ratio consensus methods that complement CalcZAF's matrix correction engine (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). For converting externally measured k-ratios (e.g., from EDS or WDS spectrum images) into wt% compositions, CalcZAF can accept k-ratio input directly, making it useful as a post-processing step in hybrid workflows.

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** CalcZAF is Windows-only, which limits its use in cross-platform or cloud-based pipelines. It is primarily a GUI application, with batch capabilities but without the native scripting flexibility of Python or Jython. It is not a spectral front-end — it does not perform peak fitting, background subtraction, or raw spectrum processing. For full quantitative SEM-EDS analysis, it must be paired with another tool (e.g., DTSA-II, vendor software, or custom Python code) that provides peak fitting and k-ratio extraction. Published validation of CalcZAF tends to focus on the accuracy of the matrix correction models themselves rather than end-to-end SEM-EDS analytical accuracy in the DTSA-II RDEV sense.

**Costs:** Open source / freely distributed as part of the Probe Software ecosystem. Low computational burden for k-ratio conversion. Learning curve is moderate for experienced microanalysts but steeper for newcomers unfamiliar with matrix correction theory. Maintenance burden is limited to Windows platform compatibility.

## 3. Specific Questions Addressed

### (a) Per-Pixel Elemental Mapping of Spectrum-Image Datacubes

**eXSpy/HyperSpy** is the best tool for this task. Its native numpy-based datacube handling, PCA/NMF denoising, and full Python ecosystem integration make it the most natural environment for per-pixel processing of large SI datasets (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). However, for SEM-EDS bulk quantification, HyperSpy's per-pixel output is limited to Cliff–Lorimer or standardless ratios unless the user builds custom ZAF/φ(ρz) correction workflows. **DTSA-II** can also produce per-pixel quantitative compositional maps via its scripting interface, applying MLLS peak fitting and XPP matrix corrections at every pixel, but this is more computationally intensive and not as naturally datacube-oriented (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26).

### (b) Bulk-Sample Standards-Based wt% Quantification of ~0.3–0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg

**NIST DTSA-II** is the most accurate and validated choice for this scenario. The Mg Kα / Al Kα overlap (Mg Kα at 1.254 keV, Al Kα at 1.487 keV, separated by ~233 eV at an EDS resolution of ~60–70 eV FWHM in this energy range) is a moderate but analytically significant interference when Mg is a minor constituent. DTSA-II's MLLS peak fitting with measured peak references is specifically designed to deconvolve such overlaps and generate a peak-fitting residual spectrum for quality control (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 15-16, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22). The RDEV studies confirm that DTSA-II achieves ±5% relative accuracy for minor constituents in many materials (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). Donovan's EPMA textbook notes that the mass absorption coefficient for Mg Kα in different matrices (e.g., ~802 vs. ~859 cm²/g in Si, depending on the MAC database) can introduce ~1% variation in results, highlighting the importance of the correct MAC choice — an area where CalcZAF's multi-database comparison can provide additional insight (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23).

### (c) CalcZAF's Advantages for K-Ratio-to-Composition Conversion

CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion with multiple φ(ρz) model choices offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction in several scenarios: (1) when the analyst wants to assess model-dependent systematic uncertainty by comparing PAP, XPP, PROZA, and CITZAF results on the same k-ratios (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4); (2) when processing k-ratios extracted from external sources (e.g., vendor software, Python pipelines, or WDS measurements) in batch mode; (3) for per-pixel wt% maps where k-ratios have been extracted by one tool (e.g., HyperSpy or DTSA-II) and the user wants to apply a different matrix correction model; and (4) in situations where specific elements or energy ranges are known to be sensitive to the choice of correction algorithm — for example, Rickerby (1995) found that the XPP model gave the least total error when K- and L-lines were combined, while the PAP procedure was generally better for K-lines only (rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). This kind of model comparison is uniquely facilitated by CalcZAF's multi-algorithm framework.

### (d) Accuracy Evidence

- **DTSA-II:** The most extensively documented. Newbury & Ritchie (2019) demonstrated that RDEV spans less than ±5% relative for >95% of EDS analyses of major and minor constituents (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 10-13). At E₀ = 5 keV, >98% of 263 measurements across 39 elements fell within ±5% RDEV, with 82% within ±2% (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). At E₀ = 20 keV, 89% were within ±2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). Trace sensitivity extends to 0.001 mass fraction even with severe peak interference (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28).
- **CalcZAF / φ(ρz) models:** Validation is primarily through model-comparison studies. Korolyuk et al. (2009) compared ZAF, PRZ, PAP, and other models, finding that when both absorption and atomic number effects are significant, total error can reach 2–4 rel% (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2). Rickerby (1995) showed that the XPP model gave lower total error than PAP for combined K- and L-line analyses (rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). Armstrong et al. (2013) specifically documented the multi-model comparison approach for estimating uncertainties.
- **HyperSpy/eXSpy:** No published bulk-SEM-EDS accuracy benchmark comparable to the RDEV studies exists. Validation is implicit through its widespread use in STEM-EDS quantification publications (e.g., Moreira et al. 2023 for AuAg nanoparticles using Cliff–Lorimer) (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10), but these are thin-film/nanoparticle contexts rather than bulk SEM samples.

### (e) Scriptability and Automation for Analysis Pipelines

- **eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python):** Best for end-to-end automation. Native Python with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn integration. Jupyter notebooks, CI/CD pipelines, and GPU-accelerated workflows are all straightforward. Widely used in automated STEM-EDS analyses and machine-learning-augmented spectral processing (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10).
- **DTSA-II (Jython):** Scriptable via Jython, a Python implementation running on the Java Virtual Machine. Capable of automating batch analysis and per-pixel mapping through scripting (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13), but the Jython environment is less ergonomic than native Python and lacks access to the full scientific Python stack (numpy C extensions, for example). Suitable for instrument-adjacent automation but less flexible for modern data science pipelines.
- **CalcZAF (Windows GUI/batch):** The least scriptable of the three. Primarily GUI-driven, with some batch processing capability for k-ratio conversion. Not naturally suited to reproducible, scripted pipelines. Best used as a dedicated correction utility in a mixed-tool workflow.

## 4. Use-Case Recommendations

The following table maps specific analysis scenarios to the recommended tool.

| Use Case / Scenario | Recommended Tool | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes | eXSpy/HyperSpy | Best native fit for hyperspectral datacubes: Python/numpy-based, strong SI processing, denoising/decomposition workflows, and widely used in STEM-EDS map analysis. DTSA-II can do per-pixel quantitative mapping, but HyperSpy/eXSpy is the more natural datacube-analysis environment (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). |
| Bulk-sample standards-based wt% quantification of a minor element with peak overlap (e.g., 0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg) | NIST DTSA-II | Best-supported choice for rigorous SEM-EDS bulk quantification because it combines standards-based k-ratios, MLLS peak fitting, residual-spectrum inspection, and validated XPP matrix correction. Newbury & Ritchie report strong RDEV performance across known materials, making DTSA-II the most evidence-backed option for difficult overlap cases (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 15-16, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). |
| Scripted k-ratio to composition conversion with multiple phi-rho-z models | CalcZAF | CalcZAF’s main advantage is standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion with multiple correction-model choices, letting the analyst compare PAP/XPP/PRZ-CITZAF-style outcomes or assess model sensitivity on externally measured k-ratios or already-derived maps. This is where it is more flexible than DTSA-II’s built-in single-default XPP workflow (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). |
| End-to-end automated Python analysis pipeline | eXSpy/HyperSpy | Best for automation because it lives directly in the Python ecosystem and integrates naturally with numpy, scipy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, notebooks, and workflow orchestration. DTSA-II scripting is useful but less ergonomic because it is centered on Java/Jython rather than mainstream scientific Python (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). |
| Validation/accuracy benchmarking against known standards | NIST DTSA-II | Strongest published validation base among the three. DTSA-II has explicit standards-based RDEV studies on large sets of known materials, including >98% of measurements within ±5% RDEV at 5 keV and similarly strong conventional-energy performance; comparable published bulk-SEM validation is not evident for HyperSpy/eXSpy, while CalcZAF is stronger as a correction-comparison engine than an end-to-end validated SEM-EDS package (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 10-13, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28). |
| Combined workflow using all three together | eXSpy/HyperSpy + NIST DTSA-II + CalcZAF | A strong combined workflow is: use HyperSpy/eXSpy for SI ingestion, denoising, masking, and pixel/summed-spectrum handling; use DTSA-II for standards-based peak fitting and k-ratio extraction/validated SEM-EDS quantification; then use CalcZAF when you want batch post-processing of those k-ratios or to compare multiple phi-rho-z corrections on the same data. This combination exploits each tool’s comparative advantage (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). |


*Table: This table maps common SEM-EDS quantitative-analysis scenarios to the most appropriate free/open tool. It is useful for deciding when to favor datacube-native Python analysis, rigorously validated bulk quantification, or standalone multi-model matrix correction.*

## 5. Recommended Combined Workflow

For the most robust SEM-EDS quantitative analysis pipeline, a combined workflow leveraging all three tools is advisable: use **HyperSpy/eXSpy** for SI datacube ingestion, denoising (PCA/NMF), pixel masking, and region-of-interest extraction (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10); use **NIST DTSA-II** for standards-based k-ratio extraction with MLLS peak fitting and XPP-corrected quantification, taking advantage of its published accuracy benchmarks (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2); and use **CalcZAF** when you need to convert those k-ratios through multiple φ(ρz) correction models for uncertainty assessment or when comparing against independently measured EPMA k-ratios (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). This combined approach is especially valuable for challenging analyses such as minor Mg in an AlSi10Mg alloy, where the Mg Kα / Al Kα overlap demands careful peak fitting (DTSA-II), the absorption correction sensitivity should be checked across models (CalcZAF), and per-pixel wt% maps need efficient datacube processing (HyperSpy/eXSpy).

# Comparative Analysis of Three Free/Open-Source Tools for SEM-EDS Quantitative Analysis

## 1. Overview

Three free/open-source software tools are commonly used for quantitative energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis: **eXSpy/HyperSpy** (Python), **NIST DTSA-II** (Java), and **CalcZAF** (Probe Software, Windows). Each tool occupies a distinct niche in the analytical workflow, and their strengths, limitations, and validation evidence differ substantially. The comprehensive comparison is summarized in the table below.

| Feature/Criterion | eXSpy/HyperSpy | NIST DTSA-II | CalcZAF |
|---|---|---|---|

## 2. Tool-by-Tool Assessment

### 2.1 eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python)

**Best use case:** Per-pixel processing and analysis of spectrum-image (SI) datacubes, particularly for (S)TEM-EDS. HyperSpy was originally a monolithic Python library for multi-dimensional data analysis in electron microscopy; the EDS/EELS quantification functionality has been refactored into a dedicated extension package called eXSpy (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).

**Strengths:** HyperSpy/eXSpy operates natively on numpy arrays and integrates directly with the broader Python scientific ecosystem (scipy, scikit-learn, scikit-image, matplotlib). It provides built-in principal component analysis (PCA) and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) for denoising and blind source separation of spectrum images (pqac-00000021). For TEM-EDS, it implements the Cliff–Lorimer k-factor method, which has been used in published quantitative studies of bimetallic nanoparticles (pqac-00000021). It is the strongest of the three tools for automated, large-scale per-pixel spectral processing and is widely used for STEM-EDS quantitative mapping (pqac-00000020).

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** HyperSpy/eXSpy does not include a validated, built-in ZAF or φ(ρz) matrix correction engine for bulk SEM-EDS quantification, which limits its applicability for the standards-based k-ratio protocol central to rigorous SEM microanalysis (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030). Published accuracy benchmarks comparable to Newbury & Ritchie's RDEV studies for DTSA-II do not appear to exist for HyperSpy's EDS quantification. Its Cliff–Lorimer approach is appropriate for thin specimens (TEM) but does not account for the absorption and fluorescence corrections required for bulk samples.

**Costs:** Free and open source (Apache/BSD-style license). Computationally efficient for vectorized datacube operations but can demand substantial RAM for very large SI datasets. Requires familiarity with Python and package management (conda/pip), which presents a learning curve for users accustomed to GUI-based microanalysis software. Cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux).

### 2.2 NIST DTSA-II (Java)

**Best use case:** Rigorous, standards-based bulk-specimen SEM-EDS quantitative analysis following the k-ratio/matrix correction protocol, including quantitative compositional mapping of spectrum images (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030).

**Strengths:** DTSA-II implements multiple linear least squares (MLLS) peak fitting using experimentally measured peak references, enabling robust deconvolution of overlapping peaks and inspection of peak-fitting residual spectra to detect hidden constituents (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000028). It employs the XPP φ(ρz) matrix correction algorithm (Pouchou & Pichoir, 1991) as its default, using the Chantler FFAST mass absorption coefficient (MAC) database (Z ≤ 92) supplemented by Sabbatucci coefficients (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026). DTSA-II has the most extensive published accuracy validation of the three tools: Newbury & Ritchie (2024) tested 263 concentration measurements for 39 elements in 113 materials at 5 keV and found >98% within ±5% RDEV and 82% within ±2% RDEV (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). At conventional beam energies (E₀ = 20 keV), a database of 122 analyses showed 100% within ±5% RDEV and 89% within ±2% RDEV (pqac-00000002). The raw analytical total (sum of all constituents) typically falls within 0.98–1.02, serving as an independent quality check (pqac-00000000). For quantitative compositional mapping, DTSA-II applies the full standards-based quantitative analysis procedure at every pixel of a spectrum image, converting raw intensity maps to true concentration maps that remove artifacts such as the Z-dependent continuum background (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000012). Newbury & Ritchie demonstrated this with a Raney nickel alloy example where false Fe contrast in raw intensity maps was eliminated by quantitative processing (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000027).

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** Per-pixel quantitative compositional mapping is computationally intensive and requires high count statistics (~1000+ counts per pixel spectrum) for low-variance wt% maps, which can demand long acquisition times (100–10,000 s depending on pixel density) (pqac-00000027). Scripting is via Jython (Python on Java), which is functional but less ergonomic than native Python for modern data science workflows. The Java desktop application has a moderate learning curve, particularly for managing the standards archive and understanding the analytical workflow conventions (pqac-00000030). DTSA-II uses a single default matrix correction model (XPP), without the multi-model comparison capability of CalcZAF.

**Costs:** Free, open source/open access from NIST. Cross-platform (Java). Moderate computational cost for point analyses; higher for per-pixel mapping of large SI datacubes. The learning curve is moderate-to-steep, as the user must understand both the k-ratio protocol concepts and the DTSA-II software interface.

### 2.3 CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software)

**Best use case:** Standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction with the ability to select from and compare multiple φ(ρz)/ZAF correction models on the same data, particularly useful for batch processing of externally measured k-ratios or assessing model-dependent uncertainties (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000005).

**Strengths:** CalcZAF's distinguishing feature is its implementation of multiple matrix correction algorithms — including PAP, XPP, PRZ (PROZA), Armstrong/CITZAF, and others — along with multiple MAC databases (Heinrich, Henke, Chantler) (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000005). This multi-model capability allows analysts to evaluate the sensitivity of results to the choice of correction algorithm, which is particularly important in challenging analytical situations where the absorption correction is large (e.g., light elements, L-lines, low overvoltage) (pqac-00000025). Armstrong, Donovan, and Carpenter (2013) specifically documented the use of CalcZAF/TryZAF/CITZAF multi-correction-algorithm programs for estimating uncertainties and improving quantitative analysis of difficult specimens. The Donovan group has also contributed advances in dead-time calibration and k-ratio consensus methods that complement CalcZAF's matrix correction engine (pqac-00000005). For converting externally measured k-ratios (e.g., from EDS or WDS spectrum images) into wt% compositions, CalcZAF can accept k-ratio input directly, making it useful as a post-processing step in hybrid workflows.

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** CalcZAF is Windows-only, which limits its use in cross-platform or cloud-based pipelines. It is primarily a GUI application, with batch capabilities but without the native scripting flexibility of Python or Jython. It is not a spectral front-end — it does not perform peak fitting, background subtraction, or raw spectrum processing. For full quantitative SEM-EDS analysis, it must be paired with another tool (e.g., DTSA-II, vendor software, or custom Python code) that provides peak fitting and k-ratio extraction. Published validation of CalcZAF tends to focus on the accuracy of the matrix correction models themselves rather than end-to-end SEM-EDS analytical accuracy in the DTSA-II RDEV sense.

**Costs:** Open source / freely distributed as part of the Probe Software ecosystem. Low computational burden for k-ratio conversion. Learning curve is moderate for experienced microanalysts but steeper for newcomers unfamiliar with matrix correction theory. Maintenance burden is limited to Windows platform compatibility.

## 3. Specific Questions Addressed

### (a) Per-Pixel Elemental Mapping of Spectrum-Image Datacubes

**eXSpy/HyperSpy** is the best tool for this task. Its native numpy-based datacube handling, PCA/NMF denoising, and full Python ecosystem integration make it the most natural environment for per-pixel processing of large SI datasets (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). However, for SEM-EDS bulk quantification, HyperSpy's per-pixel output is limited to Cliff–Lorimer or standardless ratios unless the user builds custom ZAF/φ(ρz) correction workflows. **DTSA-II** can also produce per-pixel quantitative compositional maps via its scripting interface, applying MLLS peak fitting and XPP matrix corrections at every pixel, but this is more computationally intensive and not as naturally datacube-oriented (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000027).

### (b) Bulk-Sample Standards-Based wt% Quantification of ~0.3–0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg

**NIST DTSA-II** is the most accurate and validated choice for this scenario. The Mg Kα / Al Kα overlap (Mg Kα at 1.254 keV, Al Kα at 1.487 keV, separated by ~233 eV at an EDS resolution of ~60–70 eV FWHM in this energy range) is a moderate but analytically significant interference when Mg is a minor constituent. DTSA-II's MLLS peak fitting with measured peak references is specifically designed to deconvolve such overlaps and generate a peak-fitting residual spectrum for quality control (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000028). The RDEV studies confirm that DTSA-II achieves ±5% relative accuracy for minor constituents in many materials (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). Donovan's EPMA textbook notes that the mass absorption coefficient for Mg Kα in different matrices (e.g., ~802 vs. ~859 cm²/g in Si, depending on the MAC database) can introduce ~1% variation in results, highlighting the importance of the correct MAC choice — an area where CalcZAF's multi-database comparison can provide additional insight (pqac-00000005).

### (c) CalcZAF's Advantages for K-Ratio-to-Composition Conversion

CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion with multiple φ(ρz) model choices offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction in several scenarios: (1) when the analyst wants to assess model-dependent systematic uncertainty by comparing PAP, XPP, PROZA, and CITZAF results on the same k-ratios (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025); (2) when processing k-ratios extracted from external sources (e.g., vendor software, Python pipelines, or WDS measurements) in batch mode; (3) for per-pixel wt% maps where k-ratios have been extracted by one tool (e.g., HyperSpy or DTSA-II) and the user wants to apply a different matrix correction model; and (4) in situations where specific elements or energy ranges are known to be sensitive to the choice of correction algorithm — for example, Rickerby (1995) found that the XPP model gave the least total error when K- and L-lines were combined, while the PAP procedure was generally better for K-lines only (pqac-00000025). This kind of model comparison is uniquely facilitated by CalcZAF's multi-algorithm framework.

### (d) Accuracy Evidence

- **DTSA-II:** The most extensively documented. Newbury & Ritchie (2019) demonstrated that RDEV spans less than ±5% relative for >95% of EDS analyses of major and minor constituents (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000004). At E₀ = 5 keV, >98% of 263 measurements across 39 elements fell within ±5% RDEV, with 82% within ±2% (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). At E₀ = 20 keV, 89% were within ±2% RDEV (pqac-00000002). Trace sensitivity extends to 0.001 mass fraction even with severe peak interference (pqac-00000009).
- **CalcZAF / φ(ρz) models:** Validation is primarily through model-comparison studies. Korolyuk et al. (2009) compared ZAF, PRZ, PAP, and other models, finding that when both absorption and atomic number effects are significant, total error can reach 2–4 rel% (pqac-00000023). Rickerby (1995) showed that the XPP model gave lower total error than PAP for combined K- and L-line analyses (pqac-00000025). Armstrong et al. (2013) specifically documented the multi-model comparison approach for estimating uncertainties.
- **HyperSpy/eXSpy:** No published bulk-SEM-EDS accuracy benchmark comparable to the RDEV studies exists. Validation is implicit through its widespread use in STEM-EDS quantification publications (e.g., Moreira et al. 2023 for AuAg nanoparticles using Cliff–Lorimer) (pqac-00000021), but these are thin-film/nanoparticle contexts rather than bulk SEM samples.

### (e) Scriptability and Automation for Analysis Pipelines

- **eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python):** Best for end-to-end automation. Native Python with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn integration. Jupyter notebooks, CI/CD pipelines, and GPU-accelerated workflows are all straightforward. Widely used in automated STEM-EDS analyses and machine-learning-augmented spectral processing (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021).
- **DTSA-II (Jython):** Scriptable via Jython, a Python implementation running on the Java Virtual Machine. Capable of automating batch analysis and per-pixel mapping through scripting (pqac-00000011), but the Jython environment is less ergonomic than native Python and lacks access to the full scientific Python stack (numpy C extensions, for example). Suitable for instrument-adjacent automation but less flexible for modern data science pipelines.
- **CalcZAF (Windows GUI/batch):** The least scriptable of the three. Primarily GUI-driven, with some batch processing capability for k-ratio conversion. Not naturally suited to reproducible, scripted pipelines. Best used as a dedicated correction utility in a mixed-tool workflow.

## 4. Use-Case Recommendations

The following table maps specific analysis scenarios to the recommended tool.

| Use Case / Scenario | Recommended Tool | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes | eXSpy/HyperSpy | Best native fit for hyperspectral datacubes: Python/numpy-based, strong SI processing, denoising/decomposition workflows, and widely used in STEM-EDS map analysis. DTSA-II can do per-pixel quantitative mapping, but HyperSpy/eXSpy is the more natural datacube-analysis environment (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| Bulk-sample standards-based wt% quantification of a minor element with peak overlap (e.g., 0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg) | NIST DTSA-II | Best-supported choice for rigorous SEM-EDS bulk quantification because it combines standards-based k-ratios, MLLS peak fitting, residual-spectrum inspection, and validated XPP matrix correction. Newbury & Ritchie report strong RDEV performance across known materials, making DTSA-II the most evidence-backed option for difficult overlap cases (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000030). |
| Scripted k-ratio to composition conversion with multiple phi-rho-z models | CalcZAF | CalcZAF’s main advantage is standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion with multiple correction-model choices, letting the analyst compare PAP/XPP/PRZ-CITZAF-style outcomes or assess model sensitivity on externally measured k-ratios or already-derived maps. This is where it is more flexible than DTSA-II’s built-in single-default XPP workflow (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). |
| End-to-end automated Python analysis pipeline | eXSpy/HyperSpy | Best for automation because it lives directly in the Python ecosystem and integrates naturally with numpy, scipy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, notebooks, and workflow orchestration. DTSA-II scripting is useful but less ergonomic because it is centered on Java/Jython rather than mainstream scientific Python (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| Validation/accuracy benchmarking against known standards | NIST DTSA-II | Strongest published validation base among the three. DTSA-II has explicit standards-based RDEV studies on large sets of known materials, including >98% of measurements within ±5% RDEV at 5 keV and similarly strong conventional-energy performance; comparable published bulk-SEM validation is not evident for HyperSpy/eXSpy, while CalcZAF is stronger as a correction-comparison engine than an end-to-end validated SEM-EDS package (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009). |
| Combined workflow using all three together | eXSpy/HyperSpy + NIST DTSA-II + CalcZAF | A strong combined workflow is: use HyperSpy/eXSpy for SI ingestion, denoising, masking, and pixel/summed-spectrum handling; use DTSA-II for standards-based peak fitting and k-ratio extraction/validated SEM-EDS quantification; then use CalcZAF when you want batch post-processing of those k-ratios or to compare multiple phi-rho-z corrections on the same data. This combination exploits each tool’s comparative advantage (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030). |


*Table: This table maps common SEM-EDS quantitative-analysis scenarios to the most appropriate free/open tool. It is useful for deciding when to favor datacube-native Python analysis, rigorously validated bulk quantification, or standalone multi-model matrix correction.*

## 5. Recommended Combined Workflow

For the most robust SEM-EDS quantitative analysis pipeline, a combined workflow leveraging all three tools is advisable: use **HyperSpy/eXSpy** for SI datacube ingestion, denoising (PCA/NMF), pixel masking, and region-of-interest extraction (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021); use **NIST DTSA-II** for standards-based k-ratio extraction with MLLS peak fitting and XPP-corrected quantification, taking advantage of its published accuracy benchmarks (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008); and use **CalcZAF** when you need to convert those k-ratios through multiple φ(ρz) correction models for uncertainty assessment or when comparing against independently measured EPMA k-ratios (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). This combined approach is especially valuable for challenging analyses such as minor Mg in an AlSi10Mg alloy, where the Mg Kα / Al Kα overlap demands careful peak fitting (DTSA-II), the absorption correction sensitivity should be checked across models (CalcZAF), and per-pixel wt% maps need efficient datacube processing (HyperSpy/eXSpy).

# Summary

This excerpt addresses spectral analysis techniques in X-ray microanalysis but does not directly discuss the three software tools (eXSpy/HyperSpy, NIST DTSA-II, or CalcZAF) specified in your question.

The excerpt focuses on **WDS (Wavelength Dispersive Spectrometry)** versus **EDS (Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy)** methodology. Key points include:

- WDS provides superior precision and detection limits (e.g., Na Kα CDL of 210 ppm vs. 1,950 ppm for EDS)
- WDS achieves ~5 eV resolution versus EDS's ~150 eV, enabling separation of closely-spaced peaks
- EDS suffers from pulse pileup requiring mathematical compensation; WDS does not
- Background correction methods (off-peak approach) are essential given continuum radiation limitations
- Spectral overlap misidentification is a known analytical hazard

# Summary

This excerpt discusses quantitative EPMA (electron probe microanalysis) fundamentals rather than comparing the three software tools requested. It covers:

**Matrix Corrections:** The φρz curve method simultaneously considers x-ray absorption and electron scattering. Critical parameters include incident electron energy, x-ray takeoff angle, and mass absorption coefficients. The table shows ~20% differences in mass absorption coefficients (e.g., "Mg Kα in Fe: Heinrich 6121 vs. Henke 5250"), causing ~1% quantitative analysis differences.

**Accuracy Definition:** "How close is the measurement to the true answer?" Standards-based analysis eliminates spectrometer/detector efficiency uncertainties but is "limited in accuracy by the performance of the various matrix corrections."

**Precision vs. Counts:** Precision depends on x-ray counting statistics; 10,000 counts yields ~1% precision; 1,000,000 counts yields ~0.1% precision.

**Validation Example:** Typical Fe, Si, Mg, Al analyses show percent variances of ±0.2% to ±1.8% against published values.

The excerpt provides context for accuracy metrics and matrix correction importance but does not compare the three named software tools.

# Summary

This excerpt provides foundational background on SEM-EDS principles relevant to quantitative analysis. It explains that the "interaction volume" (micron-scale region generating X-rays) is shaped by electron energy loss and backscattering, with size dependent on beam energy and atomic number. Monte-Carlo modeling software can predict spatial resolution of chemical analysis. 

The excerpt describes characteristic X-ray production through electron-orbital interactions and notes that "lower atomic number elements have fewer lines" with "generally stronger intensity," while higher-Z elements produce "greater variety of x-rays" creating "potential overlap of peaks"—a key challenge in interpretation.

For EDS specifically, it documents that spectral resolution is ~150 eV FWHM, making peak overlap problematic. Examples include Mn Kβ overlapping Fe Kα, and complex cascading overlaps in Ti-V-Cr alloys. The excerpt emphasizes EDS is "most often used for qualitative elemental analysis" and notes that quantitative work "may be advised to use the electron microprobe," though EDS remains necessary for small features in TEM or high-resolution SEM contexts.

**However, this excerpt does not address the three software tools, their comparative strengths/weaknesses, accuracy validation, or scriptability for automated pipelines.**

# Summary

This excerpt from Newbury and Ritchie discusses NIST DTSA-II's quantitative processing capabilities for spectrum-image (XSI) data. Key points:

**DTSA-II Strengths:**
- Produces accurate compositional maps using standards-based quantitative processing
- Employs "logarithmic three-band" encoding for concentration display: major constituents (0.1–1 mass fraction) in red-pink; minor (0.01–0.1) in green; trace (0.001–0.01) in blue
- Corrects false elemental contrast artifacts from X-ray continuum atomic number dependence
- Achieves RDEV within ±5% relative accuracy for major/minor constituents; ±50% relative for trace constituents down to 0.001 mass fraction (1,000 ppm)
- Handles severe peak overlap through iterative qualitative-quantitative analysis

**Limitations Noted:**
- The excerpt advocates for "end of 'black box' analytical software"—vendors should provide source code access, journal citations describing quantitative methods, and validation studies on reference materials
- Emphasizes need for transparency in recorded spectra/metadata and publicly available processing software with rigorous uncertainty budgets

## Summary

This excerpt from Newbury & Ritchie (2019) provides foundational context on EDS quantitative analysis. The authors establish that EDS has matured into "a fully quantitative analytical tool" capable of "match[ing] wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy" in determining major (C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, with useful accuracy extending into trace ranges "even when severe peak interference occurs."

The excerpt details the fundamental standards-based k-ratio protocol (Equation 1-2): k = I_X,unknown/I_X,standard, corrected by multiplicative ZAFc factors addressing atomic number (Z), absorption (A), characteristic fluorescence (F), and continuum fluorescence (c) effects. The authors note these corrections require iterative calculation and that properly controlled analyses typically yield raw analytical totals of 0.98-1.02.

The excerpt confirms "comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping" is possible by "recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element." However, the excerpt provided does not contain specific comparisons of the three tools (HyperSpy/eXSpy, DTSA-II, CalcZAF) or validation data addressing the detailed comparisons requested in the question.

# Summary

The excerpt presents validation data for NIST DTSA-II's quantitative EDS analysis capabilities through multiple tables showing relative deviations (RDEV) across compound standards. Key findings include:

**Accuracy Evidence for DTSA-II:** Tables 16-18 demonstrate RDEV values typically below ±5% for binary compounds (fluorides, oxides, nitrides). For example, NaF showed RDEV of 2.9%, CaF₂ showed 0.29%, and MgO showed −0.68%. The text notes that "spectrum arithmetic" tools in DTSA-II can synthesize composite spectra for testing peak-fitting performance.

**Peak Overlap Challenges:** The excerpt addresses interfering peaks, demonstrating DTSA-II's handling of closely-spaced elements (Th M4-N6 at 3.146 keV vs. U M5-N6,7 at 3.165 keV, separated by 19 eV). For 100:1 intensity ratios, RDEV values were 2% (U in Th-matrix) and −1.1% (Th in U-matrix); at 1,000:1 ratios, RDEV increased to 26% and −9.4% respectively, indicating accuracy degradation at extreme concentration ratios.

The excerpt provides published validation of DTSA-II's matrix-correction accuracy but does not compare other tools or address scriptability/automation aspects.

contexts.context: DTSA-II performs quantitative compositional mapping by applying the standard fixed measurement location quantitative analysis procedure at every pixel in a spectrum image datacube. The process uses scripting language to sequentially calculate pixel spectra. Peak intensities are extracted using Multiple Linear Least Squares (MLLS) peak fitting. For each pixel, k-ratios are calculated relative to a library of measured standards, and matrix corrections are applied to yield local elemental concentrations. This approach replaces raw X-ray intensity scales in elemental maps with calculated concentration values that can be meaningfully compared. The methodology is particularly important for minor and trace constituents where correction factors significantly affect the final compositional maps.

# Summary

This excerpt addresses compositional mapping techniques in SEM-EDS analysis. It distinguishes between **total intensity region-of-interest (ROI) mapping** and **X-ray spectrum imaging (XSI)**, where XSI records "a full EDS spectrum at each pixel" and processes it "with peak fitting, k-ratio standardization, and matrix corrections" to provide quantitative compositional information.

The text describes practical XSI data collection strategies, including dead-time selection, pixel density, and dwell time optimization. It illustrates limitations of simple intensity mapping using a manganese nodule example showing peak interference (Mn K-M2,3 at 6.490 keV overlaps Fe K-L2,3 at 6.400 keV), demonstrating why quantitative analysis methods are necessary. The excerpt identifies four key limitations of total intensity mapping, notably that it "conveys qualitative information only" and cannot resolve peak overlaps reliably without full spectral analysis and matrix corrections.

However, **the excerpt does not discuss the three specific software tools mentioned in your question** (HyperSpy/eXSpy, DTSA-II, or CalcZAF), their strengths, weaknesses, accuracy validation, computational costs, or scriptability for automated pipelines.
contexts.question: Compare three free/open software tools used for SEM-EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) quantitative analysis: (1) eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python, formerly the HyperSpy EDS module), (2) NIST DTSA-II (Java, by Ritchie/Newbury), and (3) CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software, open source). For EACH tool, identify: its best use case; strengths; weaknesses/limitations; and costs (computational cost, learning curve, licensing, platform/maintenance burden). Specifically address: (a) which tool is best for per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes; (b) which is most accurate for bulk-sample standards-based weight-percent quantification of a minor element (e.g. ~0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in an AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy, with the Mg Ka / Al Ka peak overlap); (c) when CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction (choice of phi-rho-z models) offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction, e.g. scripted/batch conversion of externally measured k-ratios or per-pixel wt% maps; (d) the accuracy evidence for each (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie RDEV studies for DTSA-II, Pouchou & Pichoir XPP, Donovan's phi-rho-z model comparisons, any published validation of HyperSpy/eXSpy EDS quantification); (e) scriptability/automation for building an automated analysis pipeline (Python vs Jython vs Windows GUI/batch). Cite published literature where possible.

This excerpt demonstrates quantitative compositional mapping using DTSA-II on spectrum-image (XSI) datasets, specifically showing a deep-sea manganese nodule and Raney nickel alloy. Key points:

**DTSA-II Application:** The text shows DTSA-II successfully correcting raw X-ray intensity maps to quantitative composition maps, eliminating false contrast artifacts from atomic-number-dependent continuum background (Figures 24.11-24.17). **Minor Element Challenge:** Fe at ~4 wt% maximum demonstrates the difficulty of displaying and interpreting minor/trace constituents—autoscaling is required for adequate contrast.

AutoEMXSp quantifies elemental compositions using a modified peak-to-background (P/B) method that corrects for geometry-induced artifacts in particle spectra. The software employs physically and empirically grounded models accounting for continuum X-ray generation, X-ray absorption, electron backscattering, and detector response. # Summary

This excerpt describes a STEM-EDS study of AuAg nanoparticles using quantitative chemical composition analysis. The authors applied the **Cliff-Lorimer approach** with standard error propagation on EDS counts obtained by azimuthal integration to measure composition gradients in 3-10 nm diameter particles.

Key methodological details:
- EDS counting levels achieved ~3,000 counts (IAu) for ~6 nm particles, yielding composition error bars of σCAu ∼0.01 in atom fraction
- Automated nanoparticle identification using cross-correlation with ideal circular contrast

# Summary

This excerpt discusses advances in X-ray microanalysis for layered structures, focusing on the φ(ρz) approach for quantitative analysis. Key points include:

**φ(ρz) Models**: The paper compares two Pouchou and Pichoir models—PAP (parabolic) and XPP (exponential)—describing depth distribution of primary ionization. The XPP model offers "increased flexibility for curve fitting and is mathematically more tractable" and was "found to give the least total error where K and L lines were included in the analysis."

**L-Series Absorption**: For thin films, unresolved L-series lines create significant errors due to absorption coefficient variations. A "weighted average mass absorption coefficient" formula is proposed to improve accuracy by accounting for L₁, L₂, L₃ fluorescence yields and Coster-Kronig transition probabilities.

**Accuracy Claims**: The φ(ρz) method is claimed to achieve "±1 nm" precision in multilayer analysis and depth resolution "comparable to that of Auger sputter profiling."

**Case Study**: Analysis of Ti-BN bilayers (10-15 nm) on silicon demonstrates the method's application to thin film quantification using iterative XPP (EDS) and PAP (WDS) calculations.

# Summary

The excerpt discusses X-ray spectrum imaging (XSI) compositional mapping using EDS, focusing on data processing and quantitative analysis challenges. It describes three mapping approaches with increasing accumulation times: (1) fast maps (10–100 counts/pixel) revealing only abundant species; (2) deeper gray-scale maps (10–100 s accumulation) enabling access to minor constituents; and (3) compositional mapping (100–10,000 s) requiring ≥1,000 counts/pixel for low-variance elemental maps. 

The text demonstrates **NIST DTSA-II's capability** for standards-based quantitative processing of XSI datacubes (Figure 21). It illustrates challenges with raw intensity mapping autoscaling, where different elements span different concentration ranges (e.g., Al: 0.995, Ni: 0.535, Fe: 0.042 mass fraction at full gray scale), causing false contrast. The excerpt emphasizes that achieving quantitative compositional maps requires adequate spectral counting statistics and demonstrates DTSA-II's application to standardized quantification. No direct comparison with HyperSpy/eXSpy or CalcZAF is provided.
contexts.question: Compare three free/open software tools used for SEM-EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) quantitative analysis: (1) eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python, formerly the HyperSpy EDS module), (2) NIST DTSA-II (Java, by Ritchie/Newbury), and (3) CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software, open source). For EACH tool, identify: its best use case; strengths; weaknesses/limitations; and costs (computational cost, learning curve, licensing, platform/maintenance burden). Specifically address: (a) which tool is best for per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes; (b) which is most accurate for bulk-sample standards-based weight-percent quantification of a minor element (e.g. ~0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in an AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy, with the Mg Ka / Al Ka peak overlap); (c) when CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction (choice of phi-rho-z models) offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction, e.g. scripted/batch conversion of externally measured k-ratios or per-pixel wt% maps; (d) the accuracy evidence for each (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie RDEV studies for DTSA-II, Pouchou & Pichoir XPP, Donovan's phi-rho-z model comparisons, any published validation of HyperSpy/eXSpy EDS quantification); (e) scriptability/automation for building an automated analysis pipeline (Python vs Jython vs Windows GUI/batch). Cite published literature where possible.

# Summary

This excerpt addresses EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) instrumentation fundamentals rather than software tools for quantitative analysis. It covers:

**Key Technical Parameters:**
- EDS time constant trade-offs: shorter constants maximize photon throughput (ideal for "elemental X-ray mapping") but broaden peaks; longer constants improve resolution for "quantitative analysis" requiring better peak definition. Example: Mn K-L₂,₃ natural width ~7 eV broadens to "122–150 eV FWHM or more" depending on time constant (Fig. 20.1 shows FWHM = 126 eV).
- Recommended beam energy: 20 keV for excitation up to 12 keV with "E₀/Eₖ > 1.5" overvoltage; lower energies (10 keV or below) for light elements (Be, B, C, N, O, F).
- Solid angle formula: Ω = A/r² (Eq. 20.1).
- Calibration using standards (Cu, Mn, Ni).

**Critical for quantitative analysis:** "same time constant be used for all measurements of unknowns and standards, especially if archived standards are used."

The excerpt does not compare the three software tools (HyperSpy/eXSpy, DTSA-II, CalcZAF) or address their validation, scriptability, or accuracy for minor element quantification.

# Summary

This excerpt from a textbook chapter on SEM/EDS quantitative analysis describes the **k-ratio/matrix correction protocol using NIST DTSA-II software** for bulk specimen analysis. 

Key points relevant to the comparison question:

**DTSA-II specifics:**
- The chapter dedicates Section 20.3 to "Examples of the k-ratio/Matrix Correction Protocol with DTSA II," including analysis of major constituents, severely overlapping peaks (Section 20.3.2), and minor constituents with peak overlap from major constituents (Section 20.3.3)
- Specifically addresses "Ba-Ti Interference" cases and complex alloy analysis (IN100, stainless steel) in Sections 20.3.4–20.4.2

**Methodology foundation:**
- Requires homogeneous specimens and identical measurement conditions (beam energy, electron dose, EDS parameters, detector solid angle, take-off angle)
- Emphasizes rigorous specimen preparation with surface roughness <100 nm rms (or <50 nm for elements below 1 keV)
- Uses EDS channel energy widths (e.g., 5 eV) for accurate peak fitting, particularly for low-energy peaks like C K-L₂,₃ (~50 eV FWHM)

However, the excerpt does **not compare eXSpy/HyperSpy, CalcZAF, or their specific strengths/weaknesses**, nor does it provide accuracy validation metrics (RDEV studies, phi-rho-z comparisons) or scriptability information needed to fully answer the comparison question.

Question: Compare three free/open software tools used for SEM-EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) quantitative analysis: (1) eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python, formerly the HyperSpy EDS module), (2) NIST DTSA-II (Java, by Ritchie/Newbury), and (3) CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software, open source). For EACH tool, identify: its best use case; strengths; weaknesses/limitations; and costs (computational cost, learning curve, licensing, platform/maintenance burden). Specifically address: (a) which tool is best for per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes; (b) which is most accurate for bulk-sample standards-based weight-percent quantification of a minor element (e.g. ~0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in an AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy, with the Mg Ka / Al Ka peak overlap); (c) when CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction (choice of phi-rho-z models) offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction, e.g. scripted/batch conversion of externally measured k-ratios or per-pixel wt% maps; (d) the accuracy evidence for each (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie RDEV studies for DTSA-II, Pouchou & Pichoir XPP, Donovan's phi-rho-z model comparisons, any published validation of HyperSpy/eXSpy EDS quantification); (e) scriptability/automation for building an automated analysis pipeline (Python vs Jython vs Windows GUI/batch). Cite published literature where possible.

# Comparative Analysis of Three Free/Open-Source Tools for SEM-EDS Quantitative Analysis

## 1. Overview

Three free/open-source software tools are commonly used for quantitative energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis: **eXSpy/HyperSpy** (Python), **NIST DTSA-II** (Java), and **CalcZAF** (Probe Software, Windows). Each tool occupies a distinct niche in the analytical workflow, and their strengths, limitations, and validation evidence differ substantially. The comprehensive comparison is summarized in the table below.

| Feature/Criterion | eXSpy/HyperSpy | NIST DTSA-II | CalcZAF |
|---|---|---|---|
| Developer/Affiliation | HyperSpy community; EDS/EELS functionality now split into eXSpy extension in the HyperSpy ecosystem; widely used in electron microscopy Python workflows (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10) | Nicholas W. M. Ritchie, Dale E. Newbury, NIST (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4) | John J. Donovan / Probe Software; rooted in EPMA community workflows (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20) |
| Language/Platform | Python; cross-platform scientific Python stack; native array/datacube workflow (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10) | Java application with scripting support; desktop program for SEM/EDS/EPMA-style workflows (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4) | Standalone Windows desktop utility focused on matrix correction and k-ratio conversion (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20) |
| License | Free/open-source (community Python package ecosystem) (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10) | Open-access/open-source NIST software (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2) | Open source / freely distributed in Probe Software ecosystem, but Windows-centric and less ecosystem-integrated than Python tools (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20) |
| Primary Use Case | Best for multidimensional spectrum-image processing, denoising, decomposition, visualization, and TEM/STEM-EDS per-pixel analysis; often used for nanoparticle or nanoscale mapping (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10) | Best for rigorous bulk-specimen SEM/EDS quantification using standards-based k-ratios, validated peak fitting, and quantitative compositional mapping (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4) | Best for standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion, model comparison, and post-processing externally measured intensities/k-ratios, especially when comparing correction algorithms (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4) |
| Quantification Method | Primarily Cliff-Lorimer/k-factor style quantification in published EDS use cases; commonly combined with summed or denoised spectra (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10) | Standards-based k-ratio protocol with iterative matrix correction; converts fitted intensities to concentrations using XPP corrections (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4) | Matrix-correction engine for converting measured k-ratios to composition; strong for trying multiple correction algorithms on same data (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2) |
| Matrix Correction Models | No strong evidence here for built-in bulk SEM ZAF/phi-rho-z workflow comparable to DTSA-II/CalcZAF; not the main reason users choose it for SEM bulk quant (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10) | Default XPP phi-rho-z correction (Pouchou & Pichoir) (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4) | Major advantage: multiple correction choices such as PAP, XPP, PRZ/PROZA, Armstrong/CITZAF, Love-Scott-style comparisons depending on configuration/version (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4) |

## 2. Tool-by-Tool Assessment

### 2.1 eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python)

**Best use case:** Per-pixel processing and analysis of spectrum-image (SI) datacubes, particularly for (S)TEM-EDS. HyperSpy was originally a monolithic Python library for multi-dimensional data analysis in electron microscopy; the EDS/EELS quantification functionality has been refactored into a dedicated extension package called eXSpy (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10).

**Strengths:** HyperSpy/eXSpy operates natively on numpy arrays and integrates directly with the broader Python scientific ecosystem (scipy, scikit-learn, scikit-image, matplotlib). It provides built-in principal component analysis (PCA) and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) for denoising and blind source separation of spectrum images (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). For TEM-EDS, it implements the Cliff–Lorimer k-factor method, which has been used in published quantitative studies of bimetallic nanoparticles (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). It is the strongest of the three tools for automated, large-scale per-pixel spectral processing and is widely used for STEM-EDS quantitative mapping (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7).

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** HyperSpy/eXSpy does not include a validated, built-in ZAF or φ(ρz) matrix correction engine for bulk SEM-EDS quantification, which limits its applicability for the standards-based k-ratio protocol central to rigorous SEM microanalysis (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Published accuracy benchmarks comparable to Newbury & Ritchie's RDEV studies for DTSA-II do not appear to exist for HyperSpy's EDS quantification. Its Cliff–Lorimer approach is appropriate for thin specimens (TEM) but does not account for the absorption and fluorescence corrections required for bulk samples.

**Costs:** Free and open source (Apache/BSD-style license). Computationally efficient for vectorized datacube operations but can demand substantial RAM for very large SI datasets. Requires familiarity with Python and package management (conda/pip), which presents a learning curve for users accustomed to GUI-based microanalysis software. Cross-platform (Windows/macOS/Linux).

### 2.2 NIST DTSA-II (Java)

**Best use case:** Rigorous, standards-based bulk-specimen SEM-EDS quantitative analysis following the k-ratio/matrix correction protocol, including quantitative compositional mapping of spectrum images (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

**Strengths:** DTSA-II implements multiple linear least squares (MLLS) peak fitting using experimentally measured peak references, enabling robust deconvolution of overlapping peaks and inspection of peak-fitting residual spectra to detect hidden constituents (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22). It employs the XPP φ(ρz) matrix correction algorithm (Pouchou & Pichoir, 1991) as its default, using the Chantler FFAST mass absorption coefficient (MAC) database (Z ≤ 92) supplemented by Sabbatucci coefficients (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). DTSA-II has the most extensive published accuracy validation of the three tools: Newbury & Ritchie (2024) tested 263 concentration measurements for 39 elements in 113 materials at 5 keV and found >98% within ±5% RDEV and 82% within ±2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). At conventional beam energies (E₀ = 20 keV), a database of 122 analyses showed 100% within ±5% RDEV and 89% within ±2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). The raw analytical total (sum of all constituents) typically falls within 0.98–1.02, serving as an independent quality check (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4). For quantitative compositional mapping, DTSA-II applies the full standards-based quantitative analysis procedure at every pixel of a spectrum image, converting raw intensity maps to true concentration maps that remove artifacts such as the Z-dependent continuum background (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26, goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 13-17). Newbury & Ritchie demonstrated this with a Raney nickel alloy example where false Fe contrast in raw intensity maps was eliminated by quantitative processing (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26).

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** Per-pixel quantitative compositional mapping is computationally intensive and requires high count statistics (~1000+ counts per pixel spectrum) for low-variance wt% maps, which can demand long acquisition times (100–10,000 s depending on pixel density) (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26). Scripting is via Jython (Python on Java), which is functional but less ergonomic than native Python for modern data science workflows. The Java desktop application has a moderate learning curve, particularly for managing the standards archive and understanding the analytical workflow conventions (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). DTSA-II uses a single default matrix correction model (XPP), without the multi-model comparison capability of CalcZAF.

**Costs:** Free, open source/open access from NIST. Cross-platform (Java). Moderate computational cost for point analyses; higher for per-pixel mapping of large SI datacubes. The learning curve is moderate-to-steep, as the user must understand both the k-ratio protocol concepts and the DTSA-II software interface.

### 2.3 CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software)

**Best use case:** Standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction with the ability to select from and compare multiple φ(ρz)/ZAF correction models on the same data, particularly useful for batch processing of externally measured k-ratios or assessing model-dependent uncertainties (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23).

**Strengths:** CalcZAF's distinguishing feature is its implementation of multiple matrix correction algorithms — including PAP, XPP, PRZ (PROZA), Armstrong/CITZAF, and others — along with multiple MAC databases (Heinrich, Henke, Chantler) (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). This multi-model capability allows analysts to evaluate the sensitivity of results to the choice of correction algorithm, which is particularly important in challenging analytical situations where the absorption correction is large (e.g., light elements, L-lines, low overvoltage) (rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). Armstrong, Donovan, and Carpenter (2013) specifically documented the use of CalcZAF/TryZAF/CITZAF multi-correction-algorithm programs for estimating uncertainties and improving quantitative analysis of difficult specimens. The Donovan group has also contributed advances in dead-time calibration and k-ratio consensus methods that complement CalcZAF's matrix correction engine (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). For converting externally measured k-ratios (e.g., from EDS or WDS spectrum images) into wt% compositions, CalcZAF can accept k-ratio input directly, making it useful as a post-processing step in hybrid workflows.

**Weaknesses/Limitations:** CalcZAF is Windows-only, which limits its use in cross-platform or cloud-based pipelines. It is primarily a GUI application, with batch capabilities but without the native scripting flexibility of Python or Jython. It is not a spectral front-end — it does not perform peak fitting, background subtraction, or raw spectrum processing. For full quantitative SEM-EDS analysis, it must be paired with another tool (e.g., DTSA-II, vendor software, or custom Python code) that provides peak fitting and k-ratio extraction. Published validation of CalcZAF tends to focus on the accuracy of the matrix correction models themselves rather than end-to-end SEM-EDS analytical accuracy in the DTSA-II RDEV sense.

**Costs:** Open source / freely distributed as part of the Probe Software ecosystem. Low computational burden for k-ratio conversion. Learning curve is moderate for experienced microanalysts but steeper for newcomers unfamiliar with matrix correction theory. Maintenance burden is limited to Windows platform compatibility.

## 3. Specific Questions Addressed

### (a) Per-Pixel Elemental Mapping of Spectrum-Image Datacubes

**eXSpy/HyperSpy** is the best tool for this task. Its native numpy-based datacube handling, PCA/NMF denoising, and full Python ecosystem integration make it the most natural environment for per-pixel processing of large SI datasets (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10). However, for SEM-EDS bulk quantification, HyperSpy's per-pixel output is limited to Cliff–Lorimer or standardless ratios unless the user builds custom ZAF/φ(ρz) correction workflows. **DTSA-II** can also produce per-pixel quantitative compositional maps via its scripting interface, applying MLLS peak fitting and XPP matrix corrections at every pixel, but this is more computationally intensive and not as naturally datacube-oriented (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 22-26).

### (b) Bulk-Sample Standards-Based wt% Quantification of ~0.3–0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg

**NIST DTSA-II** is the most accurate and validated choice for this scenario. The Mg Kα / Al Kα overlap (Mg Kα at 1.254 keV, Al Kα at 1.487 keV, separated by ~233 eV at an EDS resolution of ~60–70 eV FWHM in this energy range) is a moderate but analytically significant interference when Mg is a minor constituent. DTSA-II's MLLS peak fitting with measured peak references is specifically designed to deconvolve such overlaps and generate a peak-fitting residual spectrum for quality control (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 15-16, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 20-22). The RDEV studies confirm that DTSA-II achieves ±5% relative accuracy for minor constituents in many materials (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). Donovan's EPMA textbook notes that the mass absorption coefficient for Mg Kα in different matrices (e.g., ~802 vs. ~859 cm²/g in Si, depending on the MAC database) can introduce ~1% variation in results, highlighting the importance of the correct MAC choice — an area where CalcZAF's multi-database comparison can provide additional insight (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23).

### (c) CalcZAF's Advantages for K-Ratio-to-Composition Conversion

CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion with multiple φ(ρz) model choices offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction in several scenarios: (1) when the analyst wants to assess model-dependent systematic uncertainty by comparing PAP, XPP, PROZA, and CITZAF results on the same k-ratios (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4); (2) when processing k-ratios extracted from external sources (e.g., vendor software, Python pipelines, or WDS measurements) in batch mode; (3) for per-pixel wt% maps where k-ratios have been extracted by one tool (e.g., HyperSpy or DTSA-II) and the user wants to apply a different matrix correction model; and (4) in situations where specific elements or energy ranges are known to be sensitive to the choice of correction algorithm — for example, Rickerby (1995) found that the XPP model gave the least total error when K- and L-lines were combined, while the PAP procedure was generally better for K-lines only (rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). This kind of model comparison is uniquely facilitated by CalcZAF's multi-algorithm framework.

### (d) Accuracy Evidence

- **DTSA-II:** The most extensively documented. Newbury & Ritchie (2019) demonstrated that RDEV spans less than ±5% relative for >95% of EDS analyses of major and minor constituents (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 10-13). At E₀ = 5 keV, >98% of 263 measurements across 39 elements fell within ±5% RDEV, with 82% within ±2% (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). At E₀ = 20 keV, 89% were within ±2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). Trace sensitivity extends to 0.001 mass fraction even with severe peak interference (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 26-28).
- **CalcZAF / φ(ρz) models:** Validation is primarily through model-comparison studies. Korolyuk et al. (2009) compared ZAF, PRZ, PAP, and other models, finding that when both absorption and atomic number effects are significant, total error can reach 2–4 rel% (korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2). Rickerby (1995) showed that the XPP model gave lower total error than PAP for combined K- and L-line analyses (rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). Armstrong et al. (2013) specifically documented the multi-model comparison approach for estimating uncertainties.
- **HyperSpy/eXSpy:** No published bulk-SEM-EDS accuracy benchmark comparable to the RDEV studies exists. Validation is implicit through its widespread use in STEM-EDS quantification publications (e.g., Moreira et al. 2023 for AuAg nanoparticles using Cliff–Lorimer) (moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10), but these are thin-film/nanoparticle contexts rather than bulk SEM samples.

### (e) Scriptability and Automation for Analysis Pipelines

- **eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python):** Best for end-to-end automation. Native Python with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn integration. Jupyter notebooks, CI/CD pipelines, and GPU-accelerated workflows are all straightforward. Widely used in automated STEM-EDS analyses and machine-learning-augmented spectral processing (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10).
- **DTSA-II (Jython):** Scriptable via Jython, a Python implementation running on the Java Virtual Machine. Capable of automating batch analysis and per-pixel mapping through scripting (goldstein2017compositionalmapping pages 10-13), but the Jython environment is less ergonomic than native Python and lacks access to the full scientific Python stack (numpy C extensions, for example). Suitable for instrument-adjacent automation but less flexible for modern data science pipelines.
- **CalcZAF (Windows GUI/batch):** The least scriptable of the three. Primarily GUI-driven, with some batch processing capability for k-ratio conversion. Not naturally suited to reproducible, scripted pipelines. Best used as a dedicated correction utility in a mixed-tool workflow.

## 5. Recommended Combined Workflow

For the most robust SEM-EDS quantitative analysis pipeline, a combined workflow leveraging all three tools is advisable: use **HyperSpy/eXSpy** for SI datacube ingestion, denoising (PCA/NMF), pixel masking, and region-of-interest extraction (moreira2022quantitativemeasurementof pages 1-7, moreira2023agsurfacesegregation pages 5-10); use **NIST DTSA-II** for standards-based k-ratio extraction with MLLS peak fitting and XPP-corrected quantification, taking advantage of its published accuracy benchmarks (newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 3-4, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2019electronexcitedxraymicroanalysis pages 1-2); and use **CalcZAF** when you need to convert those k-ratios through multiple φ(ρz) correction models for uncertainty assessment or when comparing against independently measured EPMA k-ratios (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23, korolyuk2009accuracyinthe pages 1-2, rickerby1995progressinthe pages 1-4). This combined approach is especially valuable for challenging analyses such as minor Mg in an AlSi10Mg alloy, where the Mg Kα / Al Kα overlap demands careful peak fitting (DTSA-II), the absorption correction sensitivity should be checked across models (CalcZAF), and per-pixel wt% maps need efficient datacube processing (HyperSpy/eXSpy).
