| Language/Platform | Python; cross-platform scientific Python stack; native array/datacube workflow (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Java application with scripting support; desktop program for SEM/EDS/EPMA-style workflows (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030) | Standalone Windows desktop utility focused on matrix correction and k-ratio conversion (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022) |
| License | Free/open-source (community Python package ecosystem) (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Open-access/open-source NIST software (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008) | Open source / freely distributed in Probe Software ecosystem, but Windows-centric and less ecosystem-integrated than Python tools (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022) |
| Primary Use Case | Best for multidimensional spectrum-image processing, denoising, decomposition, visualization, and TEM/STEM-EDS per-pixel analysis; often used for nanoparticle or nanoscale mapping (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Best for rigorous bulk-specimen SEM/EDS quantification using standards-based k-ratios, validated peak fitting, and quantitative compositional mapping (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000030) | Best for standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion, model comparison, and post-processing externally measured intensities/k-ratios, especially when comparing correction algorithms (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025) |
| Quantification Method | Primarily Cliff-Lorimer/k-factor style quantification in published EDS use cases; commonly combined with summed or denoised spectra (pqac-00000021) | Standards-based k-ratio protocol with iterative matrix correction; converts fitted intensities to concentrations using XPP corrections (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030) | Matrix-correction engine for converting measured k-ratios to composition; strong for trying multiple correction algorithms on same data (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| Matrix Correction Models | No strong evidence here for built-in bulk SEM ZAF/phi-rho-z workflow comparable to DTSA-II/CalcZAF; not the main reason users choose it for SEM bulk quant (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Default XPP phi-rho-z correction (Pouchou & Pichoir) (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000025) | Major advantage: multiple correction choices such as PAP, XPP, PRZ/PROZA, Armstrong/CITZAF, Love-Scott-style comparisons depending on configuration/version (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025) |
| Peak Fitting Approach | Flexible Python-side spectral modeling/processing; often paired with PCA/NMF and custom workflows; less literature validation for bulk SEM overlap handling than DTSA-II (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Multiple linear least squares peak fitting with measured peak references; specifically emphasized as key to resolving severe overlaps and inspecting residual spectra (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000028) | Generally assumes externally obtained, already corrected/interpreted k-ratios or intensities; not primarily the spectral fitting front-end (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| Mass Absorption Coefficients | Depends on user workflow/packages; no validated SEM-bulk default MAC framework identified here (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Uses Chantler FFAST MAC database to Z<=92 and Sabbatucci values above that in reported studies (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000026) | Useful where analysts want to compare sensitivity to MAC/correction choices across algorithms/databases (e.g., Heinrich vs Henke-type values discussed in Donovan EPMA context) (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022) |
| Per-Pixel SI Mapping | Strongest option of the three for native datacube handling and pixelwise processing in Python; especially attractive for large spectrum-image pipelines (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Can do rigorous per-pixel quantitative compositional mapping, but typically with heavier processing and longer acquisition/count requirements for low-noise wt% maps (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000027) | Not a datacube-native mapper; best used after k-ratios/maps already exist and need matrix correction conversion (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| Standards-Based Quantification | Possible only insofar as user builds such workflow; not the best-established package here for rigorous bulk SEM standards-based quantification (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Core strength; explicitly built around standards-based k-ratio/matrix-correction bulk analysis (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030) | Strong for standards-based post-processing once k-ratios are measured; especially useful when those k-ratios originate outside the program (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| Scriptability/Automation | Best overall: native Python, NumPy/scikit-image/scikit-learn ecosystem, easy integration into modern automation/ML pipelines (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Scriptable, but via Java/Jython environment; capable for automation yet less convenient than mainstream Python data science stacks (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000030) | More limited/Windows-GUI-centered; practical for batch correction tasks but less natural for end-to-end reproducible pipelines than Python (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022) |
| Published Accuracy Validation | Good evidence of practical use in STEM-EDS papers, but little published bulk-SEM validation comparable to DTSA-II RDEV studies; strongest evidence is utility, not benchmarked SEM bulk accuracy (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Best published validation of the three for SEM/EDS bulk quant: >98% within ±5% RDEV at 5 keV; all results within ±5% RDEV in one 20 keV database; strong literature base by Newbury & Ritchie (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004) | Validation strength comes from comparative matrix-correction methodology rather than full spectral-end-to-end SEM/EDS studies; useful for estimating algorithm sensitivity and uncertainty (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025) |
| Learning Curve | Moderate if user already knows Python; steeper for microscopy users unfamiliar with coding, but documentation/notebooks ecosystem helps (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Moderate-to-steep: analytical concepts plus DTSA-II-specific workflow, standards archive handling, and scripting conventions (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030) | Moderate for experienced microanalysts; steeper for newcomers because concepts center on matrix-correction theory and Windows-style EPMA conventions (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022) |
| Computational Cost | Efficient for vectorized datacube work but large SI datasets can demand substantial RAM/CPU; scales well with Python scientific stack (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Point quantification is modest; per-pixel quantitative mapping becomes computationally and acquisition-time intensive, especially aiming for ~1000 counts/pixel for low-variance maps (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000027) | Usually low computational burden for post hoc k-ratio conversion; lighter than full spectral fitting/mapping tools (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023) |
| Platform/Maintenance Burden | Requires maintaining Python environment/dependencies; best for users comfortable with package management and scripting (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | Requires Java-era desktop environment and DTSA-II-specific setup; mature but less modern ecosystem feel than Python (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000030) | Windows-only burden is highest for cross-platform labs; simpler if only used as a dedicated correction utility on a single workstation (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022) |


*Table: This table compares eXSpy/HyperSpy, NIST DTSA-II, and CalcZAF across the main decision criteria relevant to SEM-EDS quantitative analysis. It is useful for matching each tool to bulk quantification, per-pixel mapping, or scripted post-processing workflows.*
artifacts.artifact-01:
| Use Case / Scenario | Recommended Tool | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes | eXSpy/HyperSpy | Best native fit for hyperspectral datacubes: Python/numpy-based, strong SI processing, denoising/decomposition workflows, and widely used in STEM-EDS map analysis. DTSA-II can do per-pixel quantitative mapping, but HyperSpy/eXSpy is the more natural datacube-analysis environment (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| Bulk-sample standards-based wt% quantification of a minor element with peak overlap (e.g., 0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in AlSi10Mg) | NIST DTSA-II | Best-supported choice for rigorous SEM-EDS bulk quantification because it combines standards-based k-ratios, MLLS peak fitting, residual-spectrum inspection, and validated XPP matrix correction. Newbury & Ritchie report strong RDEV performance across known materials, making DTSA-II the most evidence-backed option for difficult overlap cases (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000030). |
| Scripted k-ratio to composition conversion with multiple phi-rho-z models | CalcZAF | CalcZAF’s main advantage is standalone k-ratio-to-composition conversion with multiple correction-model choices, letting the analyst compare PAP/XPP/PRZ-CITZAF-style outcomes or assess model sensitivity on externally measured k-ratios or already-derived maps. This is where it is more flexible than DTSA-II’s built-in single-default XPP workflow (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). |
| End-to-end automated Python analysis pipeline | eXSpy/HyperSpy | Best for automation because it lives directly in the Python ecosystem and integrates naturally with numpy, scipy, scikit-image, scikit-learn, notebooks, and workflow orchestration. DTSA-II scripting is useful but less ergonomic because it is centered on Java/Jython rather than mainstream scientific Python (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). |
| Validation/accuracy benchmarking against known standards | NIST DTSA-II | Strongest published validation base among the three. DTSA-II has explicit standards-based RDEV studies on large sets of known materials, including >98% of measurements within ±5% RDEV at 5 keV and similarly strong conventional-energy performance; comparable published bulk-SEM validation is not evident for HyperSpy/eXSpy, while CalcZAF is stronger as a correction-comparison engine than an end-to-end validated SEM-EDS package (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009). |
| Combined workflow using all three together | eXSpy/HyperSpy + NIST DTSA-II + CalcZAF | A strong combined workflow is: use HyperSpy/eXSpy for SI ingestion, denoising, masking, and pixel/summed-spectrum handling; use DTSA-II for standards-based peak fitting and k-ratio extraction/validated SEM-EDS quantification; then use CalcZAF when you want batch post-processing of those k-ratios or to compare multiple phi-rho-z corrections on the same data. This combination exploits each tool’s comparative advantage (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000030). |


*Table: This table maps common SEM-EDS quantitative-analysis scenarios to the most appropriate free/open tool. It is useful for deciding when to favor datacube-native Python analysis, rigorously validated bulk quantification, or standalone multi-model matrix correction.*

info.query: Compare three free/open software tools used for SEM-EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) quantitative analysis: (1) eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python, formerly the HyperSpy EDS module), (2) NIST DTSA-II (Java, by Ritchie/Newbury), and (3) CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software, open source). For EACH tool, identify: its best use case; strengths; weaknesses/limitations; and costs (computational cost, learning curve, licensing, platform/maintenance burden). Specifically address: (a) which tool is best for per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes; (b) which is most accurate for bulk-sample standards-based weight-percent quantification of a minor element (e.g. ~0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in an AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy, with the Mg Ka / Al Ka peak overlap); (c) when CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction (choice of phi-rho-z models) offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction, e.g. scripted/batch conversion of externally measured k-ratios or per-pixel wt% maps; (d) the accuracy evidence for each (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie RDEV studies for DTSA-II, Pouchou & Pichoir XPP, Donovan's phi-rho-z model comparisons, any published validation of HyperSpy/eXSpy EDS quantification); (e) scriptability/automation for building an automated analysis pipeline (Python vs Jython vs Windows GUI/batch). Cite published literature where possible.

task: Compare three free/open software tools used for SEM-EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) quantitative analysis: (1) eXSpy/HyperSpy (Python, formerly the HyperSpy EDS module), (2) NIST DTSA-II (Java, by Ritchie/Newbury), and (3) CalcZAF (John Donovan, Probe Software, open source). For EACH tool, identify: its best use case; strengths; weaknesses/limitations; and costs (computational cost, learning curve, licensing, platform/maintenance burden). Specifically address: (a) which tool is best for per-pixel elemental mapping of spectrum-image datacubes; (b) which is most accurate for bulk-sample standards-based weight-percent quantification of a minor element (e.g. ~0.3-0.5 wt% Mg in an AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy, with the Mg Ka / Al Ka peak overlap); (c) when CalcZAF's standalone k-ratio-to-composition matrix correction (choice of phi-rho-z models) offers advantages over DTSA-II's built-in XPP correction, e.g. scripted/batch conversion of externally measured k-ratios or per-pixel wt% maps; (d) the accuracy evidence for each (e.g. Newbury & Ritchie RDEV studies for DTSA-II, Pouchou & Pichoir XPP, Donovan's phi-rho-z model comparisons, any published validation of HyperSpy/eXSpy EDS quantification); (e) scriptability/automation for building an automated analysis pipeline (Python vs Jython vs Windows GUI/batch). Cite published literature where possible.
